title: How to Calculate Your Grant Win Rate (2026 Benchmarks)
summary: Learn how to calculate your nonprofit’s grant win rate, benchmark it against real data (1 in 7 grants), and use the number to build a smarter grants program.
body_markdown:
According to Instrumentl’s data from 5,000+ nonprofits, the average organization wins approximately 1 in 7 grants it applies for, which equals a 14% win rate. Most grant seekers and development teams don’t know whether they’re above that benchmark, below it, or somewhere in between.


Win rate is one of the few metrics that tells you something real about how your grants program is performing. It’s the number that belongs in board reports, fundraising strategy conversations, and your go/no-go decisions about which funding opportunities to pursue.


In this article, we’ll walk you through how to calculate your win rate, what different patterns actually indicate, and what to do if the number isn’t where you want it.


‍


## How to Calculate Your Grant Win Rate


The formula is straightforward:


**` Grant Win Rate = (Number of Grants Awarded ÷ Number of Grants Applied For) × 100`**


When calculating your grant win rate, use a 12 to 24 month window or a full fiscal year; anything shorter and you're working with a sample size too small to tell you much. Grant portfolios have natural rhythms, with heavy submission seasons, slow quarters, and years where a single large federal grant award skews everything. A shorter window rarely gives you enough data to distinguish a real pattern from a temporary blip.


Two examples:


**Organization A** submitted 28 applications over the past year and received four awards. Win rate: 4 ÷ 28 × 100 = **14.3%** (right at the 1-in-7 average)


**Organization B** submitted 12 applications and received one award. Win rate: 1 ÷ 12 × 100 = **8.3%** (below average). At that volume and that rate, the issue is almost certainly prospect fit.


One additional calculation worth running is breaking your win rate down by funder type: federal, state, foundation, and corporate. Win rate patterns by funder category reveal where your team's time is generating returns and where it isn't.


‍


## What Your Win Rate Is Actually Telling You


Win rate is a diagnostic tool. The number itself matters less than what it points to, and knowing how to read it is what makes it useful. A 14% win rate at one organization might reflect a highly competitive federal portfolio; the same number at another might signal that prospect research needs attention.


**Below 10% with high application volume:** Almost always a prospect research problem. Applying to too many poorly-fit funders spreads writing capacity thin and pulls win rate down. More proposals won’t fix this.


**Above 25% with low application volume:** You may be leaving real opportunity on the table. If your team is primarily submitting to high-confidence renewals, the win rate looks strong, but the pipeline is fragile. A team that only applies to sure things will have an enviable win rate and an underfunded organization.


**Declining year-over-year despite consistent quality:** The funder landscape may have shifted. Priorities change, new cohorts of applicants emerge, and positioning that worked three years ago may no longer land the same way. This might signal that it’s time for a prospect research refresh.


**Dramatic variation by funder type:** This is the most useful pattern. If your foundation win rate is 22% and your federal win rate is 4%, that’s a clear signal about where to concentrate resources.


‍


## Four Levers That Actually Move Your Win Rate


Most advice on improving win rate focuses on proposal quality, but that’s usually the wrong place to start.


### Lever 1: Prospect Research Quality


The single biggest driver of win rate is whether you’re applying to funders who are genuinely likely to fund you. Geographic alignment, stated programmatic priorities, historical award sizes, organizational eligibility need to be evaluated *before* a proposal is started, not after a rejection arrives.


If your team is winning fewer than 1 in 7 applications, the first question isn’t “how do we write better proposals?” It’s “are we applying to the right funders?” Strong[prospect research](https://www.instrumentl.com/blog/grant-prospect-research) is what separates a reactive grants program from a strategic one.


### Lever 2: Application Selectivity


The ROI math on a 5% win-rate application versus a 25% win-rate application, including accounting for staff time, research, and writing, is significant. Build a go/no-go decision point into your grants process. Not every RFP that looks interesting deserves a full proposal, and every proposal that doesn’t get funded is capacity that didn’t go toward a better-fit opportunity.


### Lever 3: Relationship-Building Before Applying


Funders who know your organization before reading your proposal fund at significantly higher rates than cold applications. Cultivating program officer relationships through[letters of inquiry](https://www.instrumentl.com/blog/how-to-write-letter-of-inquiries-for-grant-funding) , site visits, and funder events is slow work, but it compounds. Grant teams with consistently high win rates almost always have strong relationship practices running underneath the grant writing and proposal work.


### Lever 4: Post-Rejection Analysis


Every declined application is information. Request feedback when it’s offered. Review what you know about the organizations that were funded. Look for patterns across your declines: if the same gap appears repeatedly, it’s telling you something specific about your positioning.[Post-rejection outreach](https://www.instrumentl.com/blog/sample-grant-rejection-letters) done well also keeps the relationship alive for a future cycle.


‍


## Tracking Win Rate: The Data You Need


You can’t calculate win rate without a complete submission log. At minimum, that means tracking every application submitted, including the funder name, submission date, amount requested, outcome, decision date, and amount awarded.


A spreadsheet can hold this data, but it creates its own problems: data entry discipline deteriorates over time, funder types get inconsistently categorized, and trend analysis requires manual rebuilding each quarter. If your submission log lives across two spreadsheets and an inbox folder, your win rate is only as reliable as the last time someone updated it.
